The history of the Roman Empire is a vast and complex subject, spanning over 12 centuries. It began in 753 BC, when the city of Rome was founded by Romulus and Remus, two legendary brothers who are said to have been raised by a she-wolf. The early Roman Kingdom was ruled by a series of seven kings, with Romulus being the first and Servius Tullius being the most notable for his reforms and expansion of the city. The last king, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, was overthrown in 509 BC, marking the end of the Roman Kingdom and the beginning of the Roman Republic.

During the Roman Republic, which lasted from 509 BC to 27 BC, Rome expanded its territories through a series of conquests, including the subjugation of the Italian peninsula and the defeat of Carthage in the Punic Wars. The Republic was governed by a system of elected representatives, including consuls, senators, and tribunes, who were responsible for making laws, conducting foreign policy, and commanding the military. This period also saw the rise of prominent Roman figures, such as Julius Caesar, who played a crucial role in transforming the Republic into the Roman Empire.

The Roman Empire began with the reign of Augustus Caesar, also known as Octavian, who became the first emperor of Rome in 27 BC. Augustus established the Principate, a system of government in which the emperor held supreme power but was also responsible for the welfare of the people. He also established the Praetorian Guard, a powerful military force that served as the emperor's personal bodyguard, and reorganized the Roman calendar, creating the system of months that is still used today. Augustus' reign marked the beginning of the Pax Romana, a period of relative peace and stability that lasted for over two centuries and saw the Roman Empire reach its zenith.
